title: When you don’t need Burst
sub: Small data, branchy logic, managed dependencies, maintainability — and why the profiler comes first
cards/0/title: Jobs and Burst have a cost
cards/0/body:
What marks a senior is not having rewritten everything in Burst, but knowing where it pays off. The cost has three parts:

  • scheduling — copying the job struct, the queue, waking threads, Complete(); in the Editor, safety system checks on top;
  • moving data — if the data lives in objects, every frame it is gathered into a NativeArray and scattered back, and the main thread does that;
  • code — the HPC# subset, a second data model, manual Dispose(), harder debugging.

Burst wins big on tight loops over arrays of numbers. If gathering and scattering around such a loop take longer than the loop itself, those are what you speed up — for example with a TransformAccessArray, or by keeping the data in native arrays permanently.
cards/1/body:
With a dozen elements the work is cheaper than queueing it. There is no magic threshold — only a measurement gives you one — but the options are known:

  • plain C# — often the right answer: simpler and no slower;
  • the same Burst job via Run() — Burst code, but no queue and no threads;
  • a static [BurstCompile] method called directly — Burst without jobs; parameters follow the native call rules: numbers and pointers, structs by ref/in, no generics and no NativeArray.

Jobs on several threads pay off when there is a lot of work and the main thread is busy with its own in the meantime.
cards/2/q: An inventory has 16 slots, and every frame each one gets its tooltip recomputed. A colleague suggests an IJobParallelFor with [BurstCompile]. What do you say?
cards/2/options/0: Keep plain C#: 16 elements are cheaper to compute than to queue — and first check in the Profiler that it even shows up
cards/2/options/1: Agree: Burst speeds up any code
cards/2/options/2: Use an IJobParallelFor with batchSize = 1 so each slot gets its own thread
cards/2/options/3: Move the computation into a SharedStatic to avoid copying data
cards/2/explain: At 16 elements scheduling costs more than the work, and tooltips usually pull in strings and UI that Burst does not have. If the Profiler shows it is a hot spot, first ask why it is recomputed every frame.
cards/2/wrong/1: Burst speeds up numeric loops over unmanaged data; it does not remove scheduling overhead.
cards/2/wrong/2: 16 tiny batches mean paying for work stealing 16 times and getting almost nothing.
cards/2/wrong/3: A SharedStatic is a shared static; it has nothing to do with how fast the computation runs.
cards/3/body:
Burst gives the most where data is contiguous, branches are few and the loop can be turned into SIMD. It gives less where there are:

  • lots of branches — each iteration takes its own path, there is nothing to vectorize;
  • traversal by reference — trees and graphs of objects: the time goes into cache misses, not computation;
  • managed dependencies — strings, events, UI, LINQ, GetComponent, FindObjectsByType every frame: that code cannot move into Burst, and moving the data costs more than you would gain.

The rule: move the numeric core into Burst, not the whole system. Decision logic stays in ordinary C#; heavy math over arrays goes into a job.
cards/4/q: What is worth moving into a Burst job first? Select all that apply.
cards/4/options/1: Testing 20 000 points against the camera frustum
cards/4/options/2: Parsing a JSON config when a level loads
cards/4/options/3: Dialogue logic with strings and UI events
cards/4/options/4: Generating a 1024×1024 height map from noise
cards/4/explain: Particles, the frustum and noise are tight numeric loops over arrays: exactly what Burst is for. JSON is parsed once at load time and is all strings. Dialogue is branches, strings and UI, with managed dependencies on every line.
cards/5/body:
Burst code lives by its own rules: unmanaged data only, containers with manual Dispose(), a second copy of the state next to the objects, debugging by turning Burst off or with a native debugger. Everyone who touches the system has to know all that.

To keep the cost reasonable:

  • a thin shell outside, a Burst core inside — the rest of the game sees an ordinary C# API;
  • one owner for the buffers — whoever allocates them frees them;
  • the core is pure math with no Unity API: with Burst off, the same code runs as ordinary C#, and it is easy to cover with a test.

If the gain is a fraction of a millisecond in a non-critical system, the honest call is not to rewrite it.
cards/6/body:
“Profile first, then Burst the hot loop.” The order is:

  • measure in a Development Build on the target device: in the Editor, safety checks and the Jobs Debugger are on, Burst compiles asynchronously so the first frames run managed code, and the Editor adds its own overhead. Deep Profile helps you search, but it distorts timings;
  • find where the frame goes: main thread, render thread or GPU, GC.Alloc, waiting for jobs (WaitForJobGroupID on the main thread). Burst only speeds up CPU computation;
  • estimate the ceiling: if a method takes 1 ms of 16, even an infinite speed-up saves 1 ms;
  • add your own markers and compare “before” and “after” on the same scenario.

A marker is a ProfilerMarker from Unity.Profiling. Create it once in a static readonly field and wrap the section in using (marker.Auto()) or a Begin()/End() pair. It does not allocate, shows up in the Profiler’s Hierarchy and Timeline, and works in Burst code. A Stopwatch with Debug.Log every frame is expensive in itself: a string, a log write, a stack trace — and ends up measuring itself.
cards/7/q: A frame takes 20 ms, and the AI method takes 2 ms of it. You rewrote the method in Burst and made it 10× faster. How long is the frame now?
cards/7/options/0: About 18.2 ms: the method takes 0.2 ms, 1.8 ms saved
cards/7/explain: Only the method itself gets faster: 20 − 2 + 0.2 = 18.2 ms. The other 18 ms stay as they were. That is why the profiler comes first: it shows which part of the frame is worth the effort.
cards/8/q: Profiler: Update takes 3 ms, and the Burst SteerJob takes 0.1 ms of it. Which line is the first candidate to fix?
cards/8/explain: FindObjectsByType searches the whole scene every frame and allocates a new array. The Burst job is already fast; what is expensive is everything around it: the search and the shuffling through transform. Keep the enemy list in a field and drive the transforms through a TransformAccessArray.
cards/9/task: Replace the Stopwatch and Debug.Log timing in Crowd with a profiler marker. Declare a static readonly ProfilerMarker named "Crowd.Steer" and wrap the SteerAll() call in Update in using (marker.Auto()). Add using Unity.Profiling; and remove Stopwatch and Debug.Log.
cards/9/checks/1/label: There is a static readonly ProfilerMarker named "Crowd.Steer"
cards/9/checks/2/label: In Update, the SteerAll() call is wrapped in using (marker.Auto())
cards/9/checks/3/label: The marker is not created anew in Update
cards/9/explain: The marker is created once; Auto() returns a struct that calls End() when the using block exits — no allocations. The Profiler gets a Crowd.Steer row with exact timing every frame, so “before” and “after” compare fairly. You can place the same markers inside Burst code.
cards/10/q: Put the work on a “slow” system in order.
cards/10/items/0: Make a Development Build and run it on the target device
cards/10/items/1: In the Profiler, find where the frame goes: CPU or GPU, which thread, which methods
cards/10/items/2: Put a ProfilerMarker on the suspect sections and record the “before” time
cards/10/items/3: Move the hot numeric loop into a Burst job
cards/10/items/4: Measure the same scenario again and compare with “before”
cards/10/explain: First an honest measurement where the game will actually run, then finding the hot spot, then one change, then measuring again. Without “before” there is nothing to compare, and without the profiler it is easy to speed up something that was not worth the time.
cards/11/q: Interviewer: “Why didn’t you move the whole project to Burst?” Which answer is stronger?
cards/11/options/0: Burst pays off on tight numeric loops over arrays. I profile a build first, find the hot spot and move its numeric core into Burst. Small data, branchy logic, strings and UI stay in C#: there the gain is smaller than the cost of scheduling, moving data and maintenance
cards/11/options/1: Burst does not work on mobile platforms
cards/11/options/2: Burst code is slower than plain C# below a thousand iterations
cards/11/options/3: We ran out of time: everything should be moved, it just takes long
cards/11/explain: A strong answer gives the criterion (where Burst pays off), the process (profiler first) and the cost (scheduling, data, maintenance). It shows you made an engineering decision rather than following a fashion.
cards/11/wrong/1: Burst compiles for mobile architectures too, including Arm with Neon.
cards/11/wrong/2: There is no thousand-iteration threshold; there is a scheduling cost, and a measurement shows it.
cards/11/wrong/3: Moving everything is exactly the mistake: some code only gets more complex, not faster.
